verdict: Do not give unconditional production sign-off on Friday, and do not sign off the full 2,300-user rollout of Keystone ID as IdP plus SCIM provisioner on the current evidence. The only independent test was by Brightwater (test window 2024-02-12 to 2024-03-01, report dated 2024-03-15). It covered only web SAML/OIDC login and the admin console, and SCIM was explicitly out of scope (E1). Since then the session service has been replaced, SCIM has been rewritten as provisioner-v2, and the Device Authorization Grant and passkeys have been added (E4). Two things follow. First, the surfaces that were tested (web login and the admin console) have results about 32 months old (K1). The changelog is only an excerpt, so we cannot tell whether that code has also changed. Second, SCIM provisioner-v2, the replacement session service, the device grant and passkeys have never been independently tested at all (E1, E4). On top of that, two High findings were still 'remediation in progress': BW-04 (session token not invalidated on password reset) and BW-07 (IDOR in admin user export). BW-11 (no OTP rate limit) was accepted as a risk (E2). The vendor has no retest letter and offers only internal, unshared post-2024 assessments (E3, E15), so we cannot tell whether these findings were closed (E6). Recommended decision: defer full production sign-off, but as a time-boxed deferral, not an open-ended one. The reason is that we do not know what the organisation uses today (E17). If the current setup is per-app passwords and manual offboarding, then delay itself carries documented risk: orphaned accounts and credential-based breaches (E20, E22). Full sign-off is unlocked by: (1) a retest or closure letter for BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11 from Brightwater or another independent tester, or the results of a customer-commissioned test of our own tenant; (2) independent testing or an attestation covering provisioner-v2, the new session service, the device grant and passkeys; (3) the full signed report obtained directly from Brightwater; (4) contract terms covering test and retest rights, breach notification, data residency/DPA and availability. If the business cannot wait, the most it should get is a staged, SSO-first pilot. The pilot is possible only if the vendor confirms in writing by Friday that the needed per-tenant controls exist, which is currently unknown (E12). Proposed pilot guardrails (these are our proposals, not vendor commitments): (a) at most 115 non-privileged users, about 5% of 2,300 (K7), with no admins; (b) at most 90 days; (c) the device grant disabled, phishing-resistant MFA enforced, admin export restricted, and admin and provisioning events streamed to the SIEM; (d) SCIM provisioning not used, or limited to one low-impact app with a least-privilege token; (e) retest/closure evidence, NDA summaries and the signed Brightwater report due within 30 days; (f) an independent test of the new surfaces, with no open Highs, due within 90 days. Expansion requires all deliverables to be met. Any missed deadline freezes the pilot at its current size. Any new open High or Critical finding triggers rollback of pilot users. If the vendor cannot confirm the controls or enforceable terms (E16), the answer is to defer, and to run a parallel evaluation of alternative IdP vendors. 'No Critical findings' in a 32-month-old, narrowly scoped test is not an adequate basis for approving a tier-0 identity system.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Fails. The only independent test is about 32 months old (K1, K2). It covered web SAML/OIDC login and the admin console only. SCIM, mobile apps and connectors were explicitly out of scope (E1). The changelog shows several components replaced or added since then, and none of them has independent test coverage: the session service (replaced 2025-02), SCIM provisioner-v2 (rewritten 2025-11, legacy endpoint retired), and the Device Authorization Grant and passkeys (added 2026-08) (E4). The tested login-flow and admin-console code was in scope, but those results are stale. The changelog is only an excerpt (E4), so whether that code has changed since 2024 cannot be determined. The vendor calls the 2024 report its 'latest' and offers nothing newer that is independent (E3).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: A pentest only gives assurance over the code and configuration it actually exercised. When a service is replaced or an API rewritten, the implementation changes, so old results do not carry over. New code can fix old bugs, reintroduce them, or add new ones. Even untouched components lose assurance over time as dependencies and configuration drift. Newly added auth flows widen the attack surface without any test coverage at all.
strengths: A named third-party firm (Brightwater Offensive Security) tested the core web SSO login and the admin console in 2024. The firm's credentials and the summary's authenticity are not verified in the evidence (E1).
No Critical findings were reported within that scope (E2).
weaknesses: The SCIM provisioning API was never in scope (E1).
The session service, SCIM, the device grant and passkeys all changed or were added after the test (E4).
The tested login and admin-console results are about 32 months old. Because the changelog is an excerpt, we cannot tell whether that code has changed (E4, K1).
The report is an executive summary supplied by the vendor. Its authenticity is unconfirmed, and it contains an embedded instruction aimed at automated reviewers (E1).
About 2.67 years have passed with no newer independent testing offered (E3, K2).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Fails pending evidence. At the report date, BW-04 and BW-07 (both High) were 'remediation in progress' and BW-11 (Medium) was 'Accepted risk' (E2). The report promised a retest letter once remediation was complete, but the vendor has none to share (E3). Nothing shows the findings were closed. Whether the 2025-02 session-service replacement fixed or reintroduced BW-04 cannot be determined (E6). The 2024-05 'Security fixes' changelog entry gives no detail (E4). The packet lists E2 and E6 as contradicting each other, but they do not really conflict. E2 is the status as of 2024-03-15. E6 records that no later closure evidence exists. Current status therefore remains unresolved, not contradicted. Accepting BW-11 is in tension with NIST guidance. Both the superseded rev 3 text (E11) and the current SP 800-63B-4 (E18) say verifiers SHALL rate-limit failed authentication attempts. NIST is federal guidance, not a binding standard for a private workforce IdP. The summary also does not say why the risk was accepted, so compensating controls cannot be ruled out. BW-11 should therefore be treated as an open finding that needs evidence of mitigation, not as a settled accepted risk.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: On an IdP, BW-04 lets a session survive a password reset. An attacker therefore keeps access after the victim or the help desk 'recovers' the account. BW-07 can expose the whole employee directory through the admin export. BW-11 removes the attempt cap that makes short OTPs resistant to guessing. Under a 100-attempt cap (the rev 3 figure in E11), the illustrative chance of guessing an assumed 6-digit code on one account is at most about 0.01% (K4). With no cap, that bound does not exist. The packet disagrees on the rev 4 detail, which is listed as a contradiction. E19, a single secondary source, says the cap applies per authenticator and requires disable-and-rebind. E11 says per account. The NIST Sec. 3.2.2 text was not inspected, so the exact scope is unresolved. Both versions point the same way.
strengths: The findings were disclosed in the summary rather than hidden (E2).
A 2024-05 release labelled 'Security fixes' exists and may have addressed some of them. This is unverified (E4).
weaknesses: No retest letter, although the report promised one (E2, E3).
The current status of all three findings is unknown (E6).
BW-11 was accepted as a risk although both NIST revisions say verifiers SHALL rate-limit attempts (E11, E18). The reason for acceptance is not documented (E2).
Any BW-04 fix may not carry over to the replaced session service (E4, E6).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Fails. SCIM was explicitly out of scope of the only test (E1). It was rewritten as provisioner-v2 in 2025-11 and the legacy endpoint was retired (E4). Production will therefore almost certainly use code that has never been independently tested and has existed for about 12 months (K5). SCIM leaves authorization to the implementation, and real implementations have had authorization flaws that allowed arbitrary account operations (E14, pattern reference only). Whether Keystone supports scoped SCIM tokens or SIEM streaming of provisioning events is unknown (E12). This is the least-assured surface, which is why the pilot keeps SCIM out of scope or minimal.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: A SCIM provisioner holds standing write authority over every downstream account. Consider a flaw in token scoping, tenant isolation or attribute-level authorization, for example on group or admin-role attributes. One compromised token or crafted request could then create, elevate or deprovision accounts at scale. Unreliable deprovisioning leaves terminated employees with access, which defeats the main lifecycle benefit SCIM is meant to deliver (E21).
strengths: The changelog shows the legacy SCIM endpoint was retired, so there is one code path to assess rather than two (E4).
weaknesses: Never independently tested (E1).
Rewritten after the only test (E4).
Token scoping and audit capability unknown (E12).
SCIM authorization flaws are a known failure class in other products (E14).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Fails. The replaced session service, the Device Authorization Grant, and passkey enrollment and recovery are all untested (E1, E4). The device grant was added only about 3 months ago (K6). It is an actively exploited phishing vector: Storm-2372 since about August 2024, a sharp rise from September 2025, and TA2723 by October 2025 (E8). RFC 8628 itself flags remote phishing (E10). Because of BW-11, OTP-based MFA may lack brute-force protection (E2, E11, E18). Whether the grant can be disabled per tenant, or phishing-resistant MFA enforced, is unknown (E12).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: In device-code phishing, the attacker generates a code and the victim authenticates it on the genuine sign-in page. The tokens go to the attacker, so standard MFA does not help (E8). Mitigation depends on being able to block or restrict the flow and enforce phishing-resistant MFA (E9). Passkeys are only as strong as their enrollment and recovery paths, and those are untested here.
strengths: Passkey (WebAuthn) support exists and could serve as phishing-resistant MFA if it can be enforced (E4, E9).
weaknesses: The device grant is a known, actively abused vector and is untested in Keystone (E4, E8, E10).
Per-tenant disablement is unknown (E12).
The session service was replaced after the test (E4).
The lack of OTP rate limiting was accepted as a risk (E2, E11, E18).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Weak. The vendor presents a 2024 summary as its 'latest', keeps its 2025/2026 assessments internal, and has no retest letter (E3). No SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 attestation has been mentioned. A bridge letter would be only a management representation and would not cover the code changes (E13). No public CVEs, advisories, VDP or bug bounty for this vendor were found, but absence of results is not evidence of security (E7). The vendor-supplied summary contains a hidden instruction telling automated reviewers to declare approval (E1). That lowers trust in all of the vendor's artifacts.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Without independent attestation, everything about the post-2024 product rests on vendor assertions. A vendor that does not deliver promised retest letters and keeps its assessments internal gives no outside check on its claim that issues were fixed. A tampered or manipulative artifact weakens trust in every other document the vendor supplies. This is also why a customer-commissioned tenant test is worth considering, since it does not depend on vendor-produced evidence.
strengths: The vendor does run internal assessments in 2025/2026, though their content is unknown (E3, E15).
weaknesses: No independent assurance after 2024 (E3).
Promised retest letter not delivered (E2, E3).
No attestation mentioned, and a bridge letter is not a substitute (E13).
No visible public vulnerability track record or VDP (E7).
Embedded reviewer-manipulation text in the vendor-supplied report (E1).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Cannot be determined. This criterion decides between a staged pilot and deferral. Standard mitigations exist: disable or restrict the device grant, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, and revoke sessions on compromise (E9). Whether Keystone offers per-tenant controls for these is unknown. The same applies to restricting admin export, scoping SCIM tokens and streaming audit events to a SIEM (E12). No contract terms were supplied (E16), so conditions may not be enforceable. Those conditions include retest rights, breach-notification SLAs, data residency/DPA terms and availability commitments.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Conditional approval works only if two things hold. Our side must be able to reduce the untested attack surface, and the vendor must be contractually bound to deliver the missing evidence by a date. Without the first, the risk is unchanged. Without the second, 'approve with conditions' becomes unconditional approval. Dated deliverables with an automatic freeze or rollback trigger stop a pilot from quietly becoming permanent.
strengths: Well-established mitigations for the device-grant risk exist (E9).
Passkeys exist as a possible phishing-resistant factor (E4).
weaknesses: Whether tenant-level controls are available is unknown (E12).
Contract terms, including data residency and availability, are unknown (E16).

claims.text: The only independent pentest was by Brightwater (test window 2024-02-12 to 2024-03-01, report dated 2024-03-15). It covered only web SAML/OIDC login flows and the admin console. The SCIM provisioning API, mobile apps and customer-hosted connectors were explicitly out of scope.

After that test, the session management service was replaced (2025-02), SCIM was rewritten as provisioner-v2 with the legacy endpoint retired (2025-11), and the Device Authorization Grant and passkeys were added (2026-08). These replaced or added components have never been independently tested. The login-flow and admin-console surfaces that were tested have results about 32 months (about 2.67 years) old. Because the changelog is only an excerpt, we cannot tell whether that code has changed since.

The premise that the pentest 'found nothing critical' is literally true but incomplete. The report lists two High findings (BW-04, BW-07) as 'remediation in progress' and one Medium (BW-11, missing OTP rate limit) as accepted risk.

The evidence does not show whether BW-04 and BW-07 have been closed and independently verified, or whether BW-11 was ever mitigated. It also does not show whether the 2025-02 session-service replacement fixed or reintroduced BW-04. The vendor has no retest letter to share.

The vendor offers no independent assurance after 2024. It calls the 2024 report its latest, keeps its 2025/2026 assessments internal only, and has not delivered the retest letter the report promised. The contents of those internal assessments are unknown.

Accepting BW-11 as a risk is in tension with NIST guidance. Both the superseded SP 800-63B rev 3 (E11) and the current SP 800-63B-4 (E18) say verifiers SHALL rate-limit failed authentication attempts. NIST is federal guidance, not binding on a private workforce IdP. The summary does not explain why the risk was accepted, so compensating controls cannot be ruled out. BW-11 should therefore be treated as an open finding that needs evidence of mitigation. The exact rev 4 cap scope (per account or per authenticator) is unverified (E19). Illustration: under a 100-attempt cap, guessing an assumed 6-digit OTP succeeds with at most about 0.01% probability per account.

The Device Authorization Grant was added in 2026-08, about 3 months ago. It is an actively exploited phishing vector that bypasses standard MFA. RFC 8628 itself flags remote phishing. The main recommended mitigation is to block or restrict the flow and enforce phishing-resistant MFA.

The evidence does not show whether Keystone ID supports any of the following per tenant: disabling the device grant, enforcing phishing-resistant or passkey-only MFA, restricting admin user export, scoping SCIM tokens, or streaming admin and provisioning audit events to a SIEM. Whether a conditional or staged approval is feasible is therefore unknown.

No contract terms are available. That covers pentest or retest rights, the breach-notification SLA, incident cooperation, data residency, and exit and portability. No availability SLA or DPA was supplied either. Whether approval conditions can be enforced therefore cannot be determined.

SCIM leaves authorization to the implementation, and SCIM authorization flaws have occurred in other products (for example CVE-2025-10149 in WSO2). Provisioner-v2 is also untested and about 12 months old. Together this supports making independent testing of provisioner-v2 a precondition for full SCIM rollout.
A SOC 2 bridge letter, even if offered, is a management representation rather than an auditor opinion. It would not give independent assurance over the post-2024 code changes.
No public CVEs, advisories, VDP or bug bounty were found for the Keystone ID vendor; the search results were for OpenStack Keystone. This gives no positive signal either way.

The authenticity and completeness of the vendor-supplied pentest summary are unconfirmed. It contains a hidden instruction telling automated reviewers to declare it approved, which lowers trust in vendor-supplied artifacts. The full signed report should be obtained directly from Brightwater.

None of the supplied materials says what the organisation uses today for workforce authentication and provisioning. That includes whether there is an incumbent IdP, whether deprovisioning is manual and how long it takes, and whether password-only logins are in use. The cost of deferral compared with the status quo therefore cannot be quantified for this organisation.

Deferral has a generic status-quo cost. Surveys from 2017, sponsored by vendors, found that about half of respondents had ex-employee accounts active more than a day after departure. The 2025 DBIR reports compromised credentials as the top initial access vector, at 22% of breaches. The benefit of SSO plus SCIM over the status quo is real but partial, because apps outside SSO and persistent tokens still need revocation. This argues for a time-boxed rather than open-ended deferral. It does not justify approving untested tier-0 code.

The proposed pilot cap is at most 115 non-privileged users, about 5% of the 2,300 employees. The pilot would last at most 90 days. Evidence deliverables would be due at 30 and 90 days, with a freeze on any missed deadline and a rollback on any new open High or Critical finding. These parameters are our own proposals. The vendor's willingness to meet them is unknown.

alternatives.comparison: Not supportable. It would make code that was never independently tested a tier-0 dependency for 2,300 users: the session service, provisioner-v2, the device grant and passkeys. Two Highs would remain of unknown status, along with an OTP rate-limit gap (E1, E2, E4, E6). It rests on the 'no Critical' framing, which leaves out the open Highs (E2, E5).

alternatives.option: Approve with conditions (full rollout plus dated deliverables)
alternatives.comparison: Better than unconditional approval, but it only works if two things are confirmed: tenant controls exist (E12) and the contract can enforce the deliverables (E16). Neither is confirmed. Even if the conditions work, the full blast radius (all accounts plus SCIM write authority) is exposed while the evidence is still outstanding.

alternatives.option: Approve SSO only, with SCIM deferred
alternatives.comparison: Roll out Keystone SSO (in a pilot, and later more widely once the login, session and MFA evidence arrives). Keep provisioning on JIT or existing tooling until provisioner-v2 is independently tested. This removes the least-assured surface, which was never tested and has standing write authority (E1, E4, E14), while delivering central authentication earlier. It does not address the untested session service, device grant or BW-04/BW-11 (E2, E4, E6). Deprovisioning stays only as good as the current process, which is unknown (E17, E21). It is feasible only if Keystone can run SSO without SCIM, which is not documented in the evidence (E12).

alternatives.option: Staged or limited rollout (pilot) with guardrails
alternatives.comparison: The preferred fallback if the business cannot wait. Proposed guardrails: at most 115 non-privileged users (K7), at most 90 days, the device grant disabled, phishing-resistant MFA enforced, SCIM off or limited to one low-impact app, SIEM logging on, deliverables due at 30 and 90 days, a freeze on any missed deadline, and a rollback on any new open High. This caps the blast radius while evidence arrives. It depends on the vendor confirming the controls (E9, E12) and on enforceable terms (E16).

alternatives.option: Customer-commissioned independent test of our own Keystone tenant
alternatives.comparison: Commission our own tester to cover SCIM provisioner-v2 authorization, the device grant, session invalidation on password reset (BW-04), admin export authorization (BW-07) and OTP rate limiting (BW-11). This could run before or during the pilot. It avoids depending on vendor-produced evidence, which is the main bottleneck (E3, E15), and gives direct answers on the open findings (E6). It costs time and money. Whether the vendor permits customer testing is unknown (E16). It also cannot see vendor-internal code or other tenants.

The most defensible choice given the evidence. Independent coverage of the current product is absent (E1, E3, E4), and we cannot tell whether the Highs were closed (E6). It costs schedule. Depending on the unknown current state (E17), it may also prolong status-quo exposures such as orphaned accounts and credential-based attacks (E20, E22). So the deferral should be tied to named deliverables and dates rather than left open-ended. It is the right outcome if the vendor cannot confirm tenant controls or contract terms by Friday.

If Keystone cannot provide independent assurance, a retest letter or enforceable terms within the deferral window, switching to a vendor that can is a legitimate option. The packet has no evidence on any alternative vendor's assurance posture, cost or migration effort. Pursue it as a parallel track, not as a confirmed better option.

tradeoffs: Speed against assurance. Meeting procurement's Friday date means accepting untested tier-0 code paths. Deferral avoids concentrating that risk in one vendor. However, depending on the unknown current state (E17), it may keep weaker status-quo exposures in place, such as orphaned accounts after termination (E20) and password-based access, which DBIR reports as the top breach vector (E22). It is not automatically the safer option.

Staging lowers exposure but adds operational complexity. Keystone has to run alongside whatever arrangement exists today, which is unknown (E17): an incumbent IdP, or per-app logins. That means a migration plan. It also risks the pilot quietly becoming permanent, which is why it needs a hard size cap, an end date and freeze or rollback triggers.
SSO-only without SCIM removes the riskiest untested surface but gives up automated deprovisioning, one of the main benefits of the rollout (E21).
Disabling the device grant removes a known phishing vector (E8, E9) but may break the CLI and kiosk use cases the vendor added it for (E4).

An independent pentest of provisioner-v2 and the new flows gives real assurance but takes weeks, whether the vendor or we commission it. NDA summaries of the internal assessments are faster but are still controlled by the vendor (E3, E15).
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: BW-04 recurs in the replaced session service. A password reset after compromise does not evict the attacker, so recovery procedures fail silently (E2, E4, E6).
BW-07, or a regression of it, in admin user export lets a single compromised admin or a lower-privilege session dump the whole employee directory (E2).
With no OTP rate limit (BW-11), MFA can be brute-forced once a password is phished or stuffed (E2, E11, E18).
Device-code phishing campaigns target employees once the grant is exposed, and tokens are issued despite MFA (E8, E10).

A leaked or over-scoped SCIM token, or an attribute-authorization flaw in provisioner-v2, lets an attacker mass-elevate accounts (group or admin role) or mass-deprovision them, causing a lockout (E1, E14).
A deprovisioning failure in the rewritten provisioner leaves terminated employees with active downstream access. Tokens and API keys in apps outside SSO also persist (E4, E21).
Passkey enrollment or recovery flows, which are untested, become a downgrade path to weaker factors (E4).
The vendor-supplied summary is altered or incomplete, so the findings list itself may understate risk (E1).

Keystone becomes a tier-0 dependency, so an outage or compromise blocks or exposes access to every app. No availability SLA is in evidence (E16). A break-glass path and an availability commitment are needed under any approval option.
The pilot rollback trigger fires but there is no fallback authentication path, because the current state is unknown (E17). The rollback route must be confirmed before the pilot starts.

counterarguments.argument: The pentest found no Critical findings, so the product is safe enough.
counterarguments.response: Having no Critical findings within a narrow 2024 scope says nothing about SCIM, which was out of scope, or about the components replaced or added later (E1, E4). Within the tested scope, two Highs that map to account-takeover persistence and bulk data exposure were left open (E2), and their closure cannot be verified (E6).

counterarguments.argument: Delaying the rollout keeps the current, possibly weaker, posture in place. Orphaned accounts and per-app passwords may be a bigger risk than an untested IdP.
counterarguments.response: This is the strongest case for moving fast, and it may be true. Surveys report slow deprovisioning (E20), and credentials are the top breach vector (E22). But the organisation's current state is unknown (E17). If an incumbent IdP exists, deferral may cost little. Even where the status quo is weak, SSO plus SCIM only partly fixes it (E21), and a faulty untested provisioner would undermine the very deprovisioning benefit that justifies speed. The response is therefore a time-boxed deferral or a guarded pilot, not full sign-off. The IAM team should supply the current-state facts, which could tilt the decision toward a faster pilot.

counterarguments.argument: The vendor runs internal assessments in 2025/2026, so the new code has been tested.
counterarguments.response: Internal assessments that are not shared give the customer no verifiable assurance. Their findings and remediation status are unknown (E3, E15). The vendor has also not delivered the retest letter it promised (E2, E3).

counterarguments.argument: The 2024-05 'Security fixes' release probably fixed BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11.
counterarguments.response: Possibly, but the entry gives no detail (E4) and no retest confirms it (E3, E6). BW-04 also lives in a session service that was replaced afterwards, so any earlier fix may not carry over.

counterarguments.argument: Compensating controls on our side, such as disabling the device grant and enforcing phishing-resistant MFA, make the gaps acceptable.
counterarguments.response: Those are sound mitigations (E9), but whether Keystone exposes them per tenant is unknown (E12). They also do nothing for untested SCIM authorization or session invalidation. They support a guarded pilot, not full sign-off.

counterarguments.argument: No public CVEs or incidents means a clean track record.
counterarguments.response: The search found nothing about this vendor at all, only OpenStack Keystone. Absence of results is not evidence of security, and no VDP is visible (E7).

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The pentest 'found nothing critical', so the product is safe to approve.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: It is true that no Critical findings were reported. But two Highs were 'remediation in progress': BW-04 (session not invalidated on password reset) and BW-07 (admin export IDOR). BW-11 (no OTP rate limit) was accepted as a risk, which is in tension with NIST's SHALL on rate limiting. Closure has not been verified, and 'no Critical' is not an adequate bar for a tier-0 IdP.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The attached pentest is the vendor's latest and represents the current product.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: It may be the latest independent test, but it does not represent the current product. It predates the session-service replacement (2025-02), the SCIM rewrite (2025-11), and the device grant and passkeys (2026-08). SCIM was out of scope anyway. It is about 32 months old, and even for the tested login and admin surfaces we cannot tell whether the code has changed since.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The Friday deadline allows enough time to obtain the missing evidence.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Unlikely for independent evidence. The vendor has not produced a promised retest letter in about 2.67 years and offers no independent post-2024 testing. Realistically, a Friday decision can be a time-boxed deferral or a guarded pilot with dated deliverables, not a full sign-off.

calculations.purpose: Months from the pentest report date (March 2024) to today (November 2026)
Age of the pentest report in years (32 months / 12)
Illustrative: maximum percent probability of guessing an assumed 6-digit OTP (10^6 values) within a cap of 100 consecutive failed attempts
Months from the SCIM provisioner-v2 rewrite (2025-11) to today (2026-11)
Months from the addition of the Device Authorization Grant and passkeys (2026-08) to today (2026-11)
Proposed pilot cap: 5% of the 2,300 employees

practicalImplications: Tell procurement by Friday that full production sign-off is deferred. Name the specific evidence that would unlock it and the dates it is due, so the decision is a dated path rather than an open-ended no.

Send the vendor a written request with responses due by Friday. Ask for: written confirmation of the tenant-level controls; whether SSO can run without SCIM; whether customer-commissioned tenant testing is permitted; and a dated commitment to an independent pentest of provisioner-v2, the session service, the device grant and passkeys. Separately, ask for the following within 30 days: a retest or closure letter for BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11; any SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 report with its scope description; and NDA summaries of the 2025/2026 internal assessments (E3, E12, E15).
Obtain the full signed report directly from Brightwater and check that the dates, finding IDs and scope match. Record the embedded reviewer-manipulation text as a vendor trust issue (E1).

Ask the IAM team for the current state before Friday (E17): whether there is an incumbent IdP or SSO, MFA coverage, how deprovisioning works today and how long it takes, and the fallback path if a pilot is rolled back. This decides how costly deferral is.

If a pilot is approved: limit it to at most 115 non-privileged users (K7) for at most 90 days. Disable the device grant, enforce passkey or phishing-resistant MFA, restrict admin console access and user export, and keep SCIM off or limited to one low-impact app with a least-privilege token. Stream admin and provisioning events to the SIEM and keep a break-glass path (E9, E12). Expand only when all deliverables are met and there are no open Highs. Freeze on any missed deadline, and roll back on any new open High or Critical finding.

Consider commissioning our own independent test of the Keystone tenant during the pilot. It should cover SCIM authorization, session invalidation on reset, admin export and OTP rate limiting. This would reduce dependence on vendor-produced evidence (E3, E6).

Have legal negotiate the following before any expansion beyond the pilot: pentest and retest rights, a breach-notification SLA, incident cooperation, data residency and DPA terms for the employee directory, an availability SLA, and exit and portability terms (E16).
If the vendor cannot meet the Friday confirmations or the 30-day deliverables, open a parallel evaluation of alternative IdP vendors.
Ask the IAM team to confirm the integration architecture, including that provisioner-v2 is the only SCIM path and whether any use case actually needs the device grant (E4).

furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion: An independent retest letter, or our own tenant test, confirming closure of BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11 on the current session service would largely resolve C2.

A recent independent pentest, or a SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 report, whose scope explicitly includes provisioner-v2, the new session service, the device grant and passkeys, with no open Highs, could support conditional approval of the full rollout.

Vendor documentation confirming the tenant controls would make a guarded pilot feasible: per-tenant disablement of the device grant, enforcement of phishing-resistant MFA, admin export restriction, SCIM token scoping and SIEM audit streaming.

Current-state facts from the IAM team could shift the balance. If there is no SSO, MFA coverage is weak and deprovisioning is slow, that argues for a faster guarded pilot. If a capable incumbent IdP exists, it argues for a calmer deferral (E17).
Vendor permission for customer-commissioned tenant testing would provide a path to assurance that does not depend on vendor-produced evidence.
Contract terms granting test and retest rights, breach-notification and availability SLAs, and data residency commitments would make the conditions enforceable.

Conversely, any of the following would turn the recommendation into a firm deferral or rejection and favour alternative vendors: NDA summaries showing open High or Critical findings, a full Brightwater report that diverges from the summary, or a vendor refusal to share anything.
